task.goal: Find a practical way to reduce false freezer-temperature alarms in a food bank while still catching genuine warming events.
hard_constraints: One technician has four days and can inspect two existing sensors and archived minute-level temperatures; no new hardware purchase.
Food may not be deliberately warmed and alarm coverage may not be disabled during staffed or unstaffed hours.
Distinguish sensor placement, door-opening transients and sensor drift; include a check that a proposed change does not mask a true sustained excursion.
task.available_resources: Two spare calibrated thermometers and staff door-opening notes.
task.expected_result: A reversible diagnosis and mitigation with a small validation plan.

source.title: Reduce the door events that generate nuisance alarms
source.proposal:
Mechanism: reduce warm-air entry through changes to routine freezer access, keeping sensor positions and alarm rules intact. Preparing pick lists outside the freezer, staging carts before opening, assigning one person to coordinate retrieval and checking that the door fully closes may reduce both false alarms and actual temperature disturbance. This is most useful when alarms follow avoidable prolonged or closely repeated openings.

On day 1, inspect the two sensor locations and compare each sensor against a colocated spare calibrated thermometer. Repeat checks after equilibration and later in the trial. Agreement locally but different doorway versus storage-zone behavior indicates a placement effect; brief peaks synchronized with door notes support door transients; persistent or changing disagreement with a reference suggests bias or possible drift. Do not interpret fewer alarms as proof that sensor drift has disappeared.

Use archived readings and notes on day 2 to identify the access patterns most associated with alarms. Agree with staff on one simple workflow change, then trial it during ordinary work on days 3–4. Keep necessary access unrestricted, avoid consolidating work into a single excessively long opening, and keep every existing alarm active during staffed and unstaffed hours. Record opening duration, approximate workload and alarm times. The technician needs staff cooperation, existing notes and ordinary observation; no new hardware or alarm integration is needed.

This is immediately reversible and preserves existing sustained-excursion detection. Its limits are staff adherence, incomplete door records and causes unrelated to access, such as refrigeration faults, poor placement or sensor drift. It may produce little benefit if door openings are already brief and well managed.
source.experiment: Compare trial periods with archived periods having similar workload and opening counts, using the unchanged alarm system as the comparator. Look for shorter cumulative door-open time and fewer brief peaks without an increase in baseline temperature, maximum temperature or recovery time. Reject the workflow if it merely shifts access into longer openings or does not reduce nuisance events. Confirm unchanged alarm settings and replay a recorded sustained excursion, or an explicitly synthetic sustained rise, through the existing logic offline. This checks continued alarm behavior without warming food; a four-day observation cannot establish long-term effectiveness.

refinement.title: Repair candidate 2: stage retrievals outside without lengthening openings
refinement.proposal: Original candidate index: 2. Its strongest practical advantage is reducing door-related disturbances while preserving existing alarm protection. Exact weakness: its suggested coordination and consolidation can turn several short retrievals into one prolonged opening, increasing warming even if alarm counts fall. Changed action: trial only outside-the-freezer preparation—finish the pick list and stage the cart before opening, retrieve one ordinary load, and fully close the door before sorting or preparing another trip. Do not batch additional loads into a longer opening. This makes the intervention specific and reversible while directly reducing avoidable open-door time. On days 1–2, keep all alarms active, compare both sensors with colocated calibrated thermometers after equilibration, swap references, and match archived temperatures to door notes. Local agreement with spatial differences supports placement effects; corroborated brief peaks linked to openings support door transients; persistent disagreement supports bias, while changing disagreement suggests possible drift. Trial the preparation change on days 3–4 only if door transients are implicated. Prerequisites are staff cooperation and a usable staging area outside the freezer. Remaining limit: four days and incomplete door notes cannot establish long-term effectiveness or exclude refrigeration faults.
refinement.experiment: Record opening durations, retrieval workload and temperature recovery during the trial; compare with ordinary retrievals of similar workload from days 1–2 and suitable archived periods. Falsify the repair if preparation leads to longer openings, higher between-opening temperatures or slower recovery, even if alarm counts decrease. Preserve sensor positions, thresholds and notification paths throughout staffed and unstaffed hours. Replay one recorded sustained excursion, or an explicitly synthetic sustained rise if none exists, through the unchanged alarm logic to confirm it still triggers at the existing threshold and timing. This checks logic without warming food; it does not establish physical sensor responsiveness. Revert the workflow if the thermal checks fail.

note: Source already warned against prolonged door openings. Refinement operationalizes this as close-before-sorting; it does not invent an absent safeguard.
